translationRepairs: His literary ability won the Gaozong Emperor's notice; he served at the Maojin Hall and was ordered to copy the Avatamsaka and Surangama Sutras.
His literary ability won the Gaozong Emperor's notice; he served at the Maoqin Hall and was ordered to copy the Avatamsaka and Surangama Sutras.
The hall name 懋勤殿 is Maoqin Hall; 'Maojin' misreads 勤 (qin), so the proposed idiomatic correction is accurate.
Through his literary skill he won the Gaozong Emperor's notice, served duty at the Maojin Hall, and was ordered to copy the Avatamsaka and Surangama Sutras.
Through his literary skill he won the Gaozong Emperor's notice, served duty at the Maoqin Hall, and was ordered to copy the Avatamsaka and Surangama Sutras.
The literal field repeats the same name error: 懋勤殿 is Maoqin Hall, with 勤 read qin rather than jin.
In the thirty-third year he was given the additional title of Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
In the thirty-third year he was given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
太子太保 is Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, whereas Junior Tutor would denote a different office; the proposed title is correct.
In the thirty-third year he was given the additional title of Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
In the thirty-third year he was given the additional title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
The literal field also mistranslates 太子太保; Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent accurately renders the title.
Yuncong said Minzhong had once asked him about the records, and that when Yuncong became involved in a lawsuit over a land purchase he had begged Minzhong to entreat Prefect Jiang Ciji on his behalf.
Yuncong said Minzhong had once asked him about the records, and that when Yuncong became involved in a lawsuit over a land purchase he had begged Minzhong to entreat Prefect Jiang Ciqi on his behalf.
The personal name 蔣賜棨 is Jiang Ciqi: 棨 is read qi, so the proposed idiomatic spelling corrects Ciji.

Yuncong said Minzhong had once asked him about the records, and that when Yuncong became involved in a lawsuit over land purchase he had begged Minzhong to entreat the prefect Jiang Ciji on his behalf.

Yuncong said Minzhong had once asked him about the records, and that when Yuncong became involved in a lawsuit over land purchase he had begged Minzhong to entreat the prefect Jiang Ciqi on his behalf.
The literal field contains the same name error; 賜棨 is Ciqi, not Ciji, and the replacement is complete and accurate.

When He Shen arrived, he interrogated Li's servants and obtained proof of his greed and extortion. Li was sentenced to death by slow slicing. He Shen memorialized that Yunnan's administration had grown lax, that many prefectures and counties showed treasury shortfalls, and that urgent rectification was required.

When He Shen arrived, he interrogated Li's servants and obtained proof of his greed and extortion. Li was sentenced to capital punishment. He Shen memorialized that Yunnan's administration had grown lax, that many prefectures and counties showed treasury shortfalls, and that urgent rectification was required.
論重闢 states that Li Shiyao was condemned to a capital penalty; it does not specify slow slicing, so the proposed idiomatic correction removes an invention.

When He Shen arrived, he interrogated Li's servants, obtained evidence of Li's greed and extortion, sentenced him to death by slow slicing, and memorialized that Yunnan's administration was lax, many prefectures and counties had treasury deficits, and urgent rectification was needed.

When He Shen arrived, he interrogated Li's servants, obtained evidence of Li's greed and extortion, sentenced him to capital punishment, and memorialized that Yunnan's administration was lax, many prefectures and counties had treasury deficits, and urgent rectification was needed.
The literal field likewise over-specifies 重闢 as slow slicing; capital punishment preserves the source's broader meaning.
At the time favor was extended to Chinese and foreign ministers; He Shen was given the title of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and appointed lecturer at the imperial lectures.
At the time favor was extended to ministers at court and in the provinces; He Shen was given the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent and appointed lecturer at the imperial lectures.
The proposal correctly renders 中外大臣 as ministers at court and in the provinces, but it leaves 太子太保 mistranslated as Junior Guardian; the complete line must use Grand Guardian.
While managing Mongol affairs, He Shen left a memorial on a serious Mongol case unsent. He was demoted one rank but kept in office.
While managing the Court of Colonial Affairs, He Shen left a memorial on a serious Mongol case unsent. He was demoted one rank but kept in office.
管理籓院 names management of the Court of Colonial Affairs, not an unspecified Mongol-affairs assignment; the institutional title is warranted.
He Shen managed Mongol affairs; in a serious Mongol case he left a memorial unsent and was demoted one rank but kept in office.
He Shen managed the Court of Colonial Affairs; in a serious Mongol case he left a memorial unsent and was demoted one rank but kept in office.
The literal field also reduces the named institution 籓院 to a subject area; Court of Colonial Affairs accurately restores the office.

He Shen had held power for a long time. Skilled at reading the Gaozong Emperor's wishes, he wielded stolen authority and made his own fortune. Those who would not attach themselves to him he watched for an opening to rouse the emperor's anger and bring them down;

He Shen had held power for a long time. Skilled at reading the Gaozong Emperor's wishes, he wielded usurped authority and acted with arbitrary power. Those who would not attach themselves to him he watched for an opening to rouse the emperor's anger and bring them down;
作威福 means exercising power arbitrarily or abusing authority, not making a fortune; the proposed idiomatic replacement restores the political sense.

He Shen held power long; skilled at reading the Gaozong Emperor's wishes, he thus wielded stolen authority and made his own fortune; those who did not attach to him, he watched for openings to rouse the emperor's anger and entrap them;

He Shen held power long; skilled at reading the Gaozong Emperor's wishes, he thus wielded usurped authority and acted with arbitrary power; those who did not attach to him, he watched for openings to rouse the emperor's anger and entrap them;
The literal field repeats the false financial sense for 作威福; 'acted with arbitrary power' accurately conveys the abuse of usurped authority.
Initially, during the Qianlong reign he was ordered to transfer to the Plain Yellow Banner. After his conviction he remained registered in the Plain Red Banner.
Initially, during the Qianlong reign he was ordered to transfer to the Plain Yellow Banner. After his conviction he was again registered in the Plain Red Banner.
Because He Shen had first been transferred into the Plain Yellow Banner, 仍隸正紅旗 after his conviction marks restoration to the Plain Red Banner, not uninterrupted registration there.
Initially, during Qianlong he was ordered to transfer to the Plain Yellow Banner; after his conviction he remained registered in the Plain Red Banner.
Initially, during Qianlong he was ordered to transfer to the Plain Yellow Banner; after his conviction he was again registered in the Plain Red Banner.
In the literal field, 改入 followed by 仍隸 likewise describes a return to the Plain Red Banner; 'again registered' resolves the contradiction in 'remained.'

The Jiaqing Emperor, because the account was sparse in detail and omitted the many rebukes Gaozong had imposed, could not serve to inform the present and transmit to posterity; Compiler Xi Yu was dismissed from office, and a special edict was issued as admonition.

The Jiaqing Emperor found the account sparse in detail and noted that it omitted the many rebukes Gaozong had imposed. Such an account could not serve to inform the present and transmit to posterity. Compiler Xi Yu was dismissed from office, and a special edict was issued as admonition.
無以信今傳後 describes the deficient biography, not the Jiaqing Emperor; the proposed sentences restore the correct subject and causal sequence.
From a supervising secretary in the Ministry of Personnel he was exceptionally promoted to academyian of the Grand Secretariat, concurrently with the rank of vice minister of Rites.
From a supervising secretary in the Ministry of Personnel he was exceptionally promoted to academician of the Grand Secretariat, concurrently with the rank of vice minister of Rites.
內閣學士 is correctly rendered as academician of the Grand Secretariat; 'academyian' is a typographical error and the proposal fixes it without altering meaning.

In the sixtieth year the Miao leader Shi Liudeng rebelled in Guizhou, disturbing Zhengda, Xiunao, and Songtao. The Hunan Miao Wu Bansheng and Shi Sanbao responded, besieging Yongshou. The emperor ordered Yunnan-Guizhou Governor-General Fu Kang'an to go suppress them.

In the sixtieth year the Miao leader Shi Liudeng rebelled in Guizhou, disturbing Zhengda, Xiunao, and Songtao. The Hunan Miao Wu Bansheng and Shi Sanbao responded, besieging Yongsui. The emperor ordered Yunnan-Guizhou Governor-General Fu Kang'an to go suppress them.
The place name 永綏 is Yongsui, not Yongshou, so the proposed idiomatic correction is directly supported by the Chinese characters.

In the sixtieth year the Miao leader Shi Liudeng rebelled in Guizhou, disturbing Zhengda, Xiunao, and Songtao; the Hunan Miao Wu Bansheng and Shi Sanbao responded, besieging Yongshou; the emperor ordered Yunnan-Guizhou Governor-General Fu Kang'an to go suppress them.

The literal field repeats the same toponym error; 永綏 supports Yongsui and not Yongshou.
He Lin was then entering the capital; when he reached Yingzhou, the Songtao bandits had already broken into Xiushan territory.
He Lin was then on his way to the capital; when he reached Qiongzhou, the Songtao bandits had already broken into Xiushan territory.
The proposal correctly treats 入京 as motion toward the capital, but it leaves the place as Yingzhou. The parallel text reads 邛州, Qiongzhou, which fits He Lin's route from Tibet through Sichuan.

五十年 inherits the Qianlong reign named at the start of Su Linga's biography; adding Qianlong prevents the idiomatic date from being ambiguous.
